front.title: Sahṛdaya Upāya Formation Manual
front.subtitle: The Path of Recognition · Sādhana School 2026–27

blocks.s: This manual is the working handbook for apprentices and mentors in Sahṛdaya Upāya, the 100-hour SLBT teacher formation of Sādhana School, October 2026 to August 2027. It gathers in one place everything you need to know about the program, from what’s expected to what’s at your discretion. It also includes translations of Sanskrit sources that speak directly to the teachings on _haṃsa_.

It is a first draft. Parts I, II and V restate the program as the prospectus describes it. Parts III and IV are the core of the haṃsa teaching: what ajapā-haṃsa is, and how a Sahṛdaya Meditation Teacher would teach it to a new group. The appendix gives the translations in full, so every verse a mentor quotes can be checked against its source.

**Reading the labels.** Three labels from the mentor guide carry through. **[Text]** means the root verse says it. **[Uddyota]** means Kṣemarāja says it in his commentary. **[Interpretation]** means it is the school's reading, and mentors should present it as such.

**Citations.** "ST 7.x" is _Svacchandatantra_ paṭala 7 in the numbering of the working translation. "HS" is the _Haṃsasāra_ in its continuous bracketed numbering. "PH" is _Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya_, "MM" _Mahārthamañjarī_, "VBh" _Vijñānabhairava_, "SK" _Spandakārikā_. Full editions are listed under Sources.

**Decisions already made and built in.** The initiation ceremony for Sahṛdaya Meditation we refer to as _haṃsa-upadeśa_, not _dīkṣā_. New students are told that cumulative results take 12 to 18 months of daily practice to notice the cumulative effects. Apprentices will lead the _upadeśa_ themselves as part of a certification exam assessed by their mentor. Leading the full three-session offering is an end-of-year project for certification to teach Sahṛdaya Meditation. The final teaching project is separate: a 60-minute specialized talk. The mentors are Jacob and Nataraj Chaitanya.

Sahṛdaya Upāya trains experienced teachers in two things at once: the practice of Sahṛdaya Meditation, and Subtle Liberation-Based Teaching (SLBT), the pedagogy that frames it. It runs 100 hours over eleven months, for an initial cohort of 14 teachers in formation.

Most teacher trainings bypass _formation_. They treat education as the accumulation of information, so a teacher can be well read and still unintegrated. Our approach has two parts. First, daily practice is non-negotiable: a teacher must first be a mature student, a _sādhaka_. Second, a teacher needs both **pedagogy** (an account of what lets insight take root) and **practicum** (rehearsal in front of a mentor, with affirming and critical feedback). That second part is the "hidden curriculum" traditions passed on by proximity to a primary teacher, and SLBT attempts to make this explicit.

_Sahṛdaya_, "one with heart," is classical aesthetics' word for the person in whom a work of art lands. **Sahṛdaya Meditation** names the practice: cultivating that receptivity toward one's own experience. **SLBT** names the frame. _Subtle_, because transmission happens in a register finer than instruction. _Liberation-based_, because a yoga that rejects the teleology of liberation is the kind of yoga we are working to dethrone.

The core claim comes from Pratyabhijñā: nothing learned is acquired from outside, but rather remembered from within. Awareness is already full, and practice adds only _avadhāna_, attention, never forceful effort. So any instruction that tasks a student with manufacturing a ‘yogic’ state works against the philosophy. Four principles organize the training, each with its own skill.

blocks.s: Two commitments run through all of these. _Akṛtaka-vimarśa_, uncontrived reflexive awareness, is the aim, and the teacher moves toward it by learning when to intervene, and when to encourage the student’s own budding wisdom. The _sahṛdaya_-community is ultimately intended to be a horizontal fellowship of peers, not a chain of dependency.
Every element of the curriculum maps to one of these, and assessment is against them.

items: **Pedagogical genealogy and cultural diagnosis.** Seeing the inherited model you teach within, and choosing a different path deliberately based on insight and understanding.
**Subtle attunement and energetic literacy.** Working with breath, posture, language and tone as instruments of transmission.
**Ethical speech and relational pedagogy.** Speaking clearly in charged situations and in secular rooms without diluting depth.
**Presence-based transmission.** Teaching without elitist performance or manipulation; the discipline of not-intervening.
**Philosophical grounding and curriculum design.** Building arcs that mirror initiation without becoming hierarchical, using the _prasiddhi–bhāvanā–rasa_ triad as a template.
**Lineage-informed creativity and cultural responsibility.** Reverence for tradition, attention to positionality, and cultivating a voice of one's own.

sections.title: What the program does not do

blocks.s: It does not make you a Sanskritist (expect about forty terms used accurately), a therapist (part of the competence is knowing when to refer), or anyone's guru. It confers no lineage authority or _adhikāra_. It supplies no students or business model, and it may, in the first year, cost you some students who came because nothing was asked of them.
The year runs from a November orientation to certification in August 2027. Immersions fill October to May, the retreat practicum is in July, and the final assessment runs July to August.

blocks.s: The whole practice fits in one sentence a new student can carry home: **your breath is already a meditation, and practice is learning to be present for it.** Paṭala 7 of the _Svacchandatantra_ never sets out a method, but with Kṣemarāja's _Uddyota_ it holds a clear theory of one. This part states that theory, then gives mentors the words, vocabulary and cautions to teach it.

A note on the name: the word _ajapā_ does not occur in the translated passages, but the idea does. ST 7.59 says the haṃsa has "none who utters it," and the _Uddyota_ on 7.56 quotes VBh 156 calling the 21,600 daily breaths "the recitation of the Goddess." "Ajapā-haṃsa" follows later usage, attested in the Tantric Upaniṣads (Padoux, _Tantric Mantras_).

items: **The breath is one pulse of letting go and taking in, at every scale.** [Text] "Śiva, by his very nature, is Haṃsa; the Sun … is Haṃsa; the Self too is declared to be Haṃsa; and the Breath is conjoined with Haṃsa" (7.29–30). [Uddyota] _Haṃsa_ is _hāna-samādāna_: exhale and inhale, the senses opening and closing, the world emitted and withdrawn. _Consequence:_ the breath is not a tool for reaching something larger; it is a close-up instance of it.

**It is already happening, without effort.** [Text] "Even when the mind is cast elsewhere and the eye let fall on something else, the breath still moves on always, wholly without effort" (7.58). _Consequence:_ there is nothing to start.

**Nobody recites it, and nobody can stop it.** [Text] "There is none who utters it, and none is found who checks it: the Haṃsa utters itself, abiding in the breast of living beings" (7.59). [Uddyota] It is _anāhata_, unstruck, and "never sets." _Consequence:_ instructions that make the student its producer ("say _ham_ as you inhale") get the direction backwards.

**The only thing you add is attention.** [Uddyota] "Only some, rich in attentiveness (_avadhāna-dhana_), enter into its reality" (on 7.59). "Dissolved" means "reposed through contemplative attention (_nibhālana_)" (on 7.56). _Consequence:_ this is the textual ground for SLBT's "practice adds only _avadhāna_."

**The breath already is the recitation, 21,600 times a day.** [Text] For the adept dissolved in the Prāṇa-Haṃsa, the breath-count "is declared to be his recitation (_japa_)" (7.56). _Consequence:_ you join a mantra that has run since birth.

**The breath is time, and one can stop being only the one counted.** [Text] The haṃsa dwells within "as Time itself, reckoning the world by its measures" (_kalābhiḥ kalayan jagat_, 7.146); one who recites or meditates on the Kāla-Haṃsa "moves about like Time" (7.210). [Uddyota] _kal_ means to count, to cast, to go and to know. _Consequence [Interpretation]:_ attending to the breath shifts you from the thing counted to the knowing that counts.

**The method is graded, and ends in uncontrived awareness.** [Text] The chapter also teaches effortful yoga (7.293, 7.217–225, "first conquer the breath," 7.315), but offers a direct option: "one established in the Supreme Reality is not afflicted by any of the Times" (7.226). [Uddyota] Even the tenfold yoga ends in _akṛtaka-vimarśa_ (on 7.293). _Consequence [Interpretation]:_ effort is early scaffolding, matching the SLBT arc toward the teacher withdrawing their own.

blocks.s: **Where the breath rests.** The haṃsa is "seated in the central breath" (verse quoted at 7.10) and "abides in the breast" (7.59). It comes to rest in the heart (_Uddyota_ on 7.118) and stands "in perfect balance" at mid-palate, the "equinox" (on 7.114). PH 18 adds the beginner's instruction: notice the breath's start and end points. For students these become the place the breath comes home to, and the still point where one direction turns into the other.

sections.title: The beginner talk, in five moves

items: **Something has been happening all day without you.** About fifteen breaths a minute, 21,600 a day. You didn't start it and can't really stop it. No one recites it; it recites itself (7.59).
**Each breath has two halves and a turn.** Letting go, taking in, and a small pause where one becomes the other: the rhythm of waking and sleeping, day and night.

**The old teachers heard a word in it.** _Haṃsa_, "swan," which also sounds like the breath: a soft "ham," a soft "sa." _Ajapā_, the prayer you don't have to say. You don't make the sound; you listen for it.
**Your one job is attention, not effort.** Only those "rich in attention" enter it. That attention is like listening to music you love: interested, relaxed, curious.
**Each breath is a moment of your life.** The breath is the body's clock. Resting with it, you're not running out of time; you're present for it.
Sit comfortably. Let the breath do whatever it is already doing.
Notice one exhale. Just one. Notice it finish.
Notice the inhale arrive on its own. You didn't call it.
Notice where the outbreath ends, and where the inbreath ends: the tiny place where out becomes in. (PH 18)
If you like, hear the two halves as a soft "ham" and "sa," without making the sound. If that feels like work, drop it.
When the mind wanders, that's fine. The breath kept going while you were away.
Close by noticing that the breath will keep going after you stop "meditating."

blocks.s: **On syllables [Interpretation].** The ST 7 passages don't say which syllable goes with which half. VBh 155 has the breath go out with _sa_ and in with _ha_; MM 56, read with its moon and sun pairing, gives the reverse. Pick one and keep it light, or skip the syllables.

These images are the material of the **peer articulation exercises**: mentees practise drawing new students into a teaching through an accessible image, then articulating the teaching that stems from it. Each image sets the marketplace view (meditation installs a state) beside the text's (tune in to what is already running). All are teaching stock except the swan, which is traditional.

items: **The refrigerator hum.** You notice it only when it clicks off. The sound "never sets" (7.59).
**Glasses on your head.** Effort makes the search worse; noticing ends it (7.58–59).
**The swing at the top of its arc.** The weightless instant comes with the rhythm, not by pushing (balance, on 7.114).
**The birder's ear.** The forest didn't get louder; attention got richer. "Rich in attentiveness" (on 7.59).
**The music you love.** Nobody concentrates on a favourite song; you're drawn in, "of its own savour" (on 7.58).
**The clock you stopped hearing.** The breath measures out a life; hearing it again frees you from being only counted (7.146, 7.210).
**The swan and the milk [traditional].** The haṃsa sips milk from water: innate discernment (_Spandapradīpikā_).

blocks.s: Longer class stories (the lighthouse keeper, two meditation students, the counting-house) are in the [mentor guide](https://claude.ai/artifact/9q7WRAhDECfiYfRWy5eTwe).

items: **Teach the public layer only.** 7.58–59 describe a breath every living being has. The tenfold yoga (7.293), nectar visualization (7.217–225), death-omens and the _Haṃsasāra_'s secret technique (HS 32–36, [53]–[54]) stay out of beginner classes.
**Make no literal promises.** The texts promise the end of old age and death (7.210; HS 39). "No longer only the one counted" is our interpretation; say so.
**Name the effort tension.** "First conquer the breath" (7.315) is in the chapter too. Reading effort as scaffolding is defensible, not the only reading.
**Mortality material needs care.** Breath-as-time lands hard on the grieving or ill; it belongs with Immersion 5.
**Don't assign syllables dogmatically.** The sources disagree.

**Correct one translation slip before quoting.** The _Spandapradīpikā_ rendering of a _Haṃsapārameśvara_ verse says mantras "attain flightlessness (fall)"; _patitvaṃ prāpnuvanti_ here means they "attain lordship."

chapters.title: Teaching new meditators: the three-session process

blocks.s: Three 90-minute sessions take a newcomer from "why meditate at all" to a received practice and a first month of honest questions. Session 1 makes the case, Session 2 gives the practice in the _haṃsa-upadeśa_, and Session 3 completes what students have met. Leading all three to a real group completes the certification (Part V).

blocks.s: The gap between Sessions 2 and 3 matters most: Session 3 works only if students bring real experience, so hold it after at least two weeks of practice.
The apprentice picks one angle, tells it as a story about the present, and always lands on the same four steps. Pick the angle you can speak to from your own life.

**Structure.** Arrival: one minute of silence, no instruction (5 min). The talk: a concrete scene, the problem, how the usual answers repeat it, the landing (40 min). A taste: the five-minute practice from Part III, without Sanskrit (10 min). Conversation in pairs, then the room: "What were you hoping meditation would do for you?" and "What did you notice just now that you weren't expecting?" (30 min). Close: name what Session 2 offers (5 min).
**The landing.**

items: The problem is not a lack of content but a model: we were taught to acquire states, skills and information, and that model now runs our inner lives.
Most meditation on the market repeats the model. It sells calm or productivity and makes you the manager of your own mind.
There is an older account. Awareness is already full and practice adds only attention. The breath is already a mantra, said about 21,600 times a day.
So Sahṛdaya Meditation trains a capacity, not a state: the capacity to be moved. Its fruit is wonder (_vismaya_, Śivasūtra 1.12), not calm.

The talk explains, in the tradition's words, why the practice works. The ceremony then gives the practice in a way that matches the theory: it does not install a mantra but wakes attention to one already sounding.
**The talk (35 min).** Each move introduces one Sanskrit word, only after students have felt what it names.

items: **_Haṃsa_****: letting go and taking in.** One pulse of release and return (_hāna-samādāna_, on 7.29).
**_Ajapā_****: the mantra no one recites.** "There is none who utters it … the Haṃsa utters itself" (7.59); it goes on "even when the mind is cast elsewhere" (7.58).
**_Japa_****: you've said it 21,600 times today.** The breath-count is "his recitation" (7.56).
**_Avadhāna_****: the only thing you add.** "Only some, rich in attentiveness, enter into its reality" (on 7.59).
**_Madhya_****: the turn.** Where the outbreath ends and the inbreath begins (PH 18); the haṃsa opens as "I am That" in the gap (MM 56).
**_Kāla_****: the breath as clock.** It "reckons the world" (7.146). Resting in it, one is no longer only the one counted (7.210, read gently).
**Why a ceremony.** Traditions mark a threshold so something ordinary can be received as significant. Nothing is added to you; you will know what you've been doing all along.

blocks.s: **The ritual (30 min).** It is called _haṃsa-upadeśa_, "the instruction in the haṃsa," and deliberately not _dīkṣā_. _Dīkṣā_ is given by an initiated guru and claims to transform the student; _upadeśa_ is honest about what is offered, an instruction that points.

_Setup:_ a table or altar with murtis (or a substitute), candle, a bowl of water, incense, and a pūjā tray. Each student receives a flower to offer at the pūjā table, alongside a folded piece of paper in which they have articulated their dedication to sustained practice.

items: **Lighting the lamp (2 min).** In silence. Light (_prakāśa_) is awareness, present before the lamp.
**Settling (5 min).** Guided noticing of where each outbreath and inbreath ends (PH 18). No technique, no control.
**The request (3 min).** Each student asks, "Please show me the haṃsa." The texts open with a request (the Goddess asks, Bhairava answers). A student may stay silent and witness.
**The verse (2 min).** The mentor recites ST 7.59: _nāsyoccārayitā kaścit pratihantā na vidyate | svayam uccarate haṃsaḥ prāṇinām urasi sthitaḥ ||_, then in English.

**The pointing (8 min).** "I am not going to give you a syllable to repeat. I am going to point to one you already say." Students rest a hand on their own chest. Over three breaths the mentor says softly, once, "haṃ… sa…", then falls silent for two to three minutes. The giving is a pointing, not a transfer.
**The offering (3 min).** Each student places their flower in the water by the lamp, with their card. "Nothing here needs anything from you. What you offer is attention."

**The commitment (3 min).** Together, aloud: "For forty days I will sit with the breath that recites itself, ten minutes each day, and bring what I notice to our next meeting." A simple _samaya_, giving the practice time to take root.
**Closing (4 min).** "You have been saying this all your life. From today you know it." The lamp stays lit into the silent sitting.

blocks.s: **Silent sitting (20 min).** The first practice as received practitioners, with no guidance after the first minute.

**Forty days, then 12 to 18 months.** The 40-day commitment is the first step, not the whole practice. Teachers say plainly in the ceremony that the cumulative results of any practice take 12 to 18 months of daily sitting to notice. They then offer the context for that longer arc: a new-practitioner cohort that meets regularly after Session 3.

**Why this is faithful [Interpretation].** Every element is traditional in kind (lamp, request, verse, offering, commitment), and every one is aimed at attention. That follows 7.59 and the _Spandapradīpikā_'s sources: mantras that are "mere letters" stay powerless; sound works only when "enriched by awareness." Left out on purpose: anything from ST 7's initiatory layer, and any claim of _śaktipāta_.
Session 3 starts from what students actually experienced. The apprentice's main skill is _paryavasāna_.

**Structure.** Reports (30 min): each student answers "What did you notice that surprised you?", and the apprentice completes the report, for example "You noticed the breath kept going while you were planning dinner. So who was breathing?" Questions and objections (45 min). Closing practice (15 min): ten minutes of silent sitting, then the invitation into the 12–18 month cohort.

blocks.s: To be certified to teach Sahṛdaya Meditation, an apprentice delivers the full three-session offering of Part IV to a test group as the end-of-year project. chapters.label: Appendix A
chapters.title: The Haṃsa in Svacchandatantra paṭala 7, with Kṣemarāja's Uddyota

blocks.s: Jacob's working translation of every Haṃsa passage in paṭala 7 (Kālādhikāra), reproduced in full and as written. Verse numbers follow the _Uddyota_ edition as transmitted in that source; cite ST 7 by the KSTS edition (ed. Madhusūdan Kaul). Passages purely on breath-arithmetic are summarized in italics by the translator.

This is the seventh chapter (_paṭala_) of the **Svacchandatantra**, "the chapter on Time" (_kālādhikāra_), together with Kṣemarāja's _Uddyota_ commentary. The chapter maps cosmic Time (_kāla_) onto the movement of the breath (_prāṇa_) in the body, and its hidden spine is the **Haṃsa** — at once (a) the gander/"wild goose," (b) the spontaneous breath-mantra _haṃ-sa_ (⇄ _so'ham_) that beings breathe without effort, and (c) a name of the supreme Lord.

Kṣemarāja's constant move is an **etymology by nirukti**: _haṃsa_ is read as **hāna + samādāna** — "abandoning and taking in." Outwardly this is exhalation and inhalation; cosmically it is _sarga-saṃhāra_, the emission and withdrawal of the universe. So to say "Śiva, the Sun, the Self, and Prāṇa are all Haṃsa" is to say that one and the same reality pulses as emission and reabsorption at every level. When that pulsing reckons and measures the world, it is **Kāla-haṃsa**, the "Time-Haṃsa," and meditation on it conquers death.

Passages are given in textual order. For each: the root verse(s) of the Tantra in transliteration and translation, followed by the _Uddyota_ commentary (translated fully where it bears on the Haṃsa, condensed where it turns to purely technical breath-timing). Bracketed material and headings are editorial.

Recurring technical vocabulary is kept close to the Sanskrit: _prāṇa_ (breath/vital energy), _apāna_ (the downward/incoming breath), _madhyama prāṇa_ (the central breath), _hāna-samādāna_ (emission-and-reception), _sarga/saṃhāra_ (emission/withdrawal), _niṣkala bhaṭṭāraka_ (the partless Lord), _anāhata_ (the "unstruck" sound), _svātantrya_ (autonomy), _vyāpti_ (pervasion), _tuṭi_ (a breath-unit of time).

In the commentary on verse 10, having explained that the body is pervaded by 350 million nāḍīs "as a palāśa leaf is pervaded by its veins," Kṣemarāja quotes a verse in which the Haṃsa first appears as the source from which the breaths radiate.

lines: madhyaprāṇaniviṣṭahaṃsavisṛtā ye romakūpāśrayāḥ prāṇāḥ sūkṣmavimarśaśālivapuṣaḥ sārdhatrikoṭyātmakāḥ | tān mantrātmatayā vilomayati yo niḥśeṣatattvāśraye dehe 'sāv iha nādabhairavatanuḥ svacchandanāthaḥ paraḥ ||

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Those breaths (_prāṇa_) that stream out from the **Haṃsa** seated in the central breath and that lodge in the pores of the skin — three and a half _crores_ [350 million] in number, their bodies made of subtle reflective awareness (_sūkṣma-vimarśa_) — he who, in this body that is the seat of the entire array of _tattvas_, turns them back in reverse as [so many forms of] mantra: he is here the Supreme Lord Svacchanda, whose very body is Bhairava as Sound (_nāda-bhairava_)."

The point of the citation: every one of the countless breaths is a filament radiating from the single Haṃsa of the central channel; the yogin who "reverses" them — reading them back to their source as mantra — _is_ Svacchandabhairava.

sections.title: 2. The keystone: Śiva, Sun, Self and Breath are all Haṃsa (7.29–30)

blocks.s: _This is the doctrinal heart of the chapter's Haṃsa teaching. The context (from 7.28) is that the breath rises and falls within the body just as the outer sun rises and sets; the verse now explains_ why _the same breath is inconstant, now going out, now coming in — because its very nature is Haṃsa, "abandoning-and-taking-in."_

lines: śivo dharmeṇa haṃsas tu sūryo haṃsaḥ prabhānvitaḥ || 7-29 || ātmā vai haṃsa ity uktaḥ prāṇo haṃsasamanvitaḥ |

blocks.s: **Translation of the verse.** "Śiva, by his very nature (_dharma_), is **Haṃsa**; the Sun, endowed with radiance, is **Haṃsa**; the Self (_ātman_) too is declared to be **Haṃsa**; and the Breath (_prāṇa_) is conjoined with **Haṃsa**."
**Commentary (****_Uddyota_****).**

"He who was earlier called **Śiva** — the dense mass of consciousness-and-bliss (_cidānanda-ghana_) — is, _by his dharma_, that is, by his innate nature which is **autonomy** (_svātantrya_), **Haṃsa**: one whose law is **abandoning-and-taking-in** (_hāna-samādāna_), the agent of the emission and withdrawal of the universe (_viśva-sarga-saṃhāra-kārī_). Precisely because he is Śiva, he performs the **fivefold cosmic act** (_pañcavidha-kṛtya_), whose essence is emission-and-reabsorption.

"And just as he is [Haṃsa], so too the **Sun** — which is made of Śiva's Power of Knowledge (_jñāna-śakti_) — being conjoined with radiance, that is, with light (_prabhā = prakāśa_), is **Haṃsa**, one whose nature is abandoning-and-taking-in, by way of the emitting and drawing-in of the fluid/nectar (_rasa-visarga-ādāna_).

"And since, by the principle already settled, the **Self** (_ātman_) is nothing but Śiva himself appearing as **contracted consciousness** through his own autonomy, it too — by way of the opening and closing of the sense-organs and the rest (_karaṇa-unmīlana-nimīlana_) — has the nature of abandoning-and-taking-in, and is therefore called **Haṃsa**.

"As it was said [at 4.260] in the connecting gloss (_yojanikā_): _'By this very conjunction/yoga the puruṣa is Haṃsa.'_ Just so, that very **Breath** — even while it rests on the plane of breath — performing abandoning-and-taking-in both outwardly and inwardly, is precisely **Haṃsa**. For this Sun, this Self, and this Breath are fully conjoined with the Haṃsa — the **partless Lord** (_niṣkala bhaṭṭāraka_) whose essence is the **unstruck** [sound] (_anāhata_), in the form of Śiva.

"For it is he alone who, by the descending sequence, having taken up the station that ends in breath, performs the outward and inward going-and-coming (_bahir-antar gamāgamau_) — and so effects emission and withdrawal. **Therefore, by the mere practice of cultivating this station, the great yogins swiftly enter the state of Supreme Śiva.** In passing, the secret meaning (_rahasyārtha_) has here been glanced at."

_Immediately after, verse 7.30 continues:_ **tasyodayāt kalet kālaḥ** — "From its (the breath's) rising, Time reckons [the world]," i.e. the breath, rising, measures out the world through the sixfold transformation (birth, subsistence, etc.), dividing it as past, present and future. The Haṃsa-breath and Time are thus the same pulse.
After computing the number of breath-movements in a day, month and year, the text describes the adept who reposes in the breath.

**Translation.** "The adept (_sādhaka_) forever **dissolved in the Prāṇa-Haṃsa** … becomes a knower of the Supreme Reality (_paratattva-vit_). For him this [breath-count] is declared to be [his true] recitation (_japa_), granting the fruits of both _siddhi_ and liberation."

**Commentary.** "_Dissolved_ (_līna_) means reposed through contemplative attention (_nibhālana_). — And thus, by his sinking down into the plane of breath he attains, through absorption into the _śākta_ station, [the state of] a **knower of the Supreme Reality**.

"Here the breath is called **Haṃsa** because it is the substrate of the Haṃsa that is the very mantra-potency (_mantra-vīrya_) of the whole universe, as determined [above]. He who is dissolved therein is thereby ever endowed with a recitation (_japa_) equal to [that great] breath-count. As is said in the **Vijñānabhairava**:

lines: 'Six hundred by day and by night, together with twenty-one thousand — this is proclaimed the recitation of the Goddess; supremely hard to attain, it lies at the end of the breath.' (VBh 156)"

blocks.s: _And 7.57 divides the fruit:_ downward flow (as far as the heart-lotus) yields _siddhi_; the upward flow, [culminating] in the Supreme Reality, yields liberation.

sections.title: 4. The middle breath is Haṃsa-natured (commentary on 7.58)

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Even when the mind is cast elsewhere and the eye let fall on something else, the breath still moves on always, wholly **without effort** (_ayatnād eva_)."

**Commentary (Haṃsa-relevant portion).** "…Even though the inner and outer faculties are spread out toward their own objects, still, for one who knows the pervasion of the breath and is intent on repose in the Supreme Reality, the **middle breath, whose self is Haṃsa** (_prāṇo haṃsātmā madhyamaḥ_), moves on of its own savour (_svarasata eva_), always, effortlessly — by that very mode that grants supreme repose."
The chapter's most celebrated line: the Haṃsa is the mantra no one recites, because it recites itself.

lines: svayam uccarate haṃsaḥ prāṇinām urasi sthitaḥ || 7-59 ||

blocks.s: **Translation.** "There is none who **utters** it, and none is found who **checks** it: the **Haṃsa utters itself** (_svayam uccarate haṃsaḥ_), abiding in the breast of living beings."

**Commentary.** "**'Haṃsa'** is the supreme **partless Lord** whose true nature was described before; and because the middle breath is presided over by it, that middle breath too has for its essence the pervasion already determined.

"**'It utters itself'** — transcending the entire sequence of signified and signifier (_vācya-vācaka-krama_), it flashes forth (_sphurati_) as the **potency of the Great Mantra** (_mahāmantra-vīrya_) whose essence is supreme non-difference. For it has none who utters it and none who checks it, since it alone, as the **agent of all** (_sarva-kartṛtva_), has the nature of the supreme Subject (_paramātṛ-rūpa_).

"For just this reason it is proclaimed **'unstruck'** (_anāhata_): unlike the other phonemes, it is not made manifest by the striking of the places and organs of articulation, and it **never sets** (_an-astamita_, is never extinguished). And this [Haṃsa] abides in the **breast, the heart**, of living beings, being **the very life even of life itself** (_jīvitasyāpi jīvita-bhūtaḥ_). Yet only some, rich in attentiveness (_avadhāna-dhana_), enter into its reality."

sections.title: 6. The Prāṇa-Haṃsa dividing day and night in the fortnight (7.77)

lines: prāṇahaṃso yadā prāptas tv adhastāṃ prathamāṃ tuṭim || 7-77 ||
pūrvam ardhaṃ tv ahaḥ proktaṃ tuṭyardham aparaṃ niśā |

blocks.s: **Translation.** "When the **Prāṇa-Haṃsa** reaches the first lower _tuṭi_, the first half [of that unit] is declared to be day, and the latter half-_tuṭi_ is night."

**Commentary.** "**'Prāṇa-Haṃsa' as before** (i.e., as already glossed). _'Lower'_ means [reckoned] from the first _tuṭi_ [above] the half-_tuṭi_ of the [fortnight-]juncture — namely the _tuṭi_ that is the first day (_pratipad_) of the bright fortnight. The division into day and night is exactly as before; and so it is to be understood of the second and subsequent lunar days as well." _(Here the Haṃsa-breath's motion through the sixteen tuṭis maps the days of the lunar fortnight.)_

sections.title: 7. The Haṃsa draws in the world's vital sap by its rays (7.101–102)

blocks.s: In the "northern course" (uttarāyaṇa), the breath rising from Capricorn to Gemini withdraws the vital essence of the world.

lines: … tatkāle saṃhared vīryaṃ jagaty asmiṃś carācare || 7-101 ||
haṃso raśmibhir ākṛṣya garbhasthaṃ kārayet tu tam |
karkaṭādeḥ samārabhya sarvaṃ varṣati tat punaḥ |

blocks.s: **Translation.** "…At that time [in the northern course] he **withdraws the vital potency** (_vīrya_) in this world of moving and unmoving things. The **Haṃsa**, drawing it in **by its rays** (_raśmibhir ākṛṣya_), makes it embryonic (_garbhastha_). And that ancient [potency], taken in and held in manifold embryonic form, it **rains forth again**, beginning from Cancer [the southern course]."

**Commentary.** "'At that time' — in the northern course. The 'increase of days' [in that course arises] from the practice of grasping the knowable, disregarding the portion of repose. **'Vīrya'** is the vital sap (_rasa_) that nourishes the universe. **'Haṃsa'** is inwardly the **unstruck Sound** (_anāhata-nāda_), and outwardly the **Sun**. **'By its rays'** — inwardly, by the goddess-faculties (_indriya-devī_) turned inward and made of reflective awareness; outwardly, by [the sun's] beams. He explains _'saṃharet'_ (withdraws): **'making it embryonic'** means [drawing it] within the [supreme] Power (_śakti_); _'kārayet'_ — he sets the rays to work drawing it in." _(The Haṃsa thus inhales the world's sap in the ascending breath and exhales it back in the descending breath — hāna-samādāna on a cosmic scale.)_

sections.title: 8. The Haṃsa kindled by illumined awareness, resting as the "Fish" in the throat (7.107–109)

blocks.s: The chapter's mantra for the "northern-course" practice: the inner unstruck sound (adhyātma-śabda), tasting the sixfold savours, becomes the mantra "Fish" (mīna) darting up in the throat.

lines: śabdasaṃvedanaṃ tasya sphuṭaṃ tatra bhaved yataḥ || 7-108 ||
tadārabhya japāt tasya sarvam eva pravartate |
mithunāntaṃ ca deveśi tataḥ siddhiḥ prajāyate || 7-109 ||

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Its self is the form of the **inner sound** (_adhyātma-śabda_); impelled by the tasting of the six savours, **kindled by the awakening that is the Haṃsa** (_haṃsa-bodha-pradīpta_), it takes up [the form of] the **Fish** (_mīna_) in the throat. Because a clear sensing of the sound then arises for him, from that point on, through his recitation, everything [he undertakes] proceeds; and [reposing] at the end of Gemini, O Queen of gods, _siddhi_ is thereupon born."

**Commentary.** "The **'inner sound'** is the unstruck resonance (_anāhata-dhvani_); its highest sense is what was settled at [7.29] _'Śiva by his nature is Haṃsa.'_ **'Kindled by the awakening that is the Haṃsa'** means enkindled by the **knowledge of pervasion** (_vyāpti-jñāna_) that is the [realized] awakening of the Haṃsa. By the pervasion of the 'turning of the Fish' already explained, it reaches the throat, the zone of the Gemini/Fish-sign's course; and taking up the darting Fish-form — by the flicking of its head-and-tail, which are the upper and lower _kalās_ [of the sixth seed-syllable] — it becomes mantra. Then, mounted upon the breath that is the seat of all the senses, urged toward the tasting of the palatal nectar, from that point on it attains mantra-hood, i.e., is [truly] uttered."

sections.title: 9. "With its Haṃsa" — the breath poised at the point-power (7.110)

blocks.s: The turn to the "southern course" (dakṣiṇāyana), the breath now descending from Cancer to Libra, raining nectar down.

**Translation.** "**Together with its Haṃsa** (_sahaṃsaḥ_), poised in the **Point-power** (_bindu-śakti_), facing downward through the doors of _siddhi_, [the breath] rains down from Cancer as far as Libra, [passing] through the region of the palate. Then the embodied one [carries it] down from the throat, spreading everywhere from the heart-lotus."

**Commentary.** "**The breath that abides together with the Haṃsa** is 'poised in the Point-power' — that is, seated in the _samanā_ station, per [6.15] _'When it enacts creation, the bindu rises up above.'_ Because it grants _siddhi_, [it descends] through those doors — the six finger-breadths and four courses; **facing downward**, it has entered within by way of the _brahmarandhra_; in the region of the palate, i.e., mid-palate, it rains as far as Libra, [reckoned as] the throat, six finger-breadths [down]. …The heart, being made to blossom by the filling of the _apāna_, has the character of a lotus; **'from the heart-lotus'** means resting upon it." _(This descending, nectar-raining Haṃsa is the counterpart to §7 above: samādāna giving way to hāna.)_

lines: śaktyadho hṛdaye haṃsaḥ saṃkramet karkaṭe priye || 7-112 ||
ṣaḍaṅgulāni saṃtyajya siṃhe vai saṃkramet punaḥ |
ṣaḍaṅgulaiḥ punas tyaktaiḥ kanyāṃ saṃkramate punaḥ || 7-113 ||
nāsikāgrāt tu tālvantaṃ tyaktvaivaṃ viṣuvad bhavet |

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Below the [supreme] Power, in the heart, the **Haṃsa** crosses into Cancer, O beloved. Abandoning six finger-breadths, it crosses again into Leo; and again, six finger-breadths given up, it crosses into Virgo. Having left [the span] from the tip of the nose to the palate, thus arises the **equinox** (_viṣuvat_): this is called the crossing into Libra — it is the **southern equinox**."

**Commentary (Haṃsa-relevant portion).** "Below the Power that is the means-of-practice lies the pervading Power (_vyāpinī-śakti_). At the station of the _brahmarandhra_ and so on, the **Haṃsa, downward-faced like a crab** (_karkaṭa iva adhovaktro haṃsaḥ_) [enters Cancer]; then, from its predominance of resonance (_nadana_) and its power to invade the whole universe, [it becomes] Leo; then, from the predominance of the point-radiance (_baindava-prakāśa_) at the brow-center, with its glow and beauty and its motion of all-pervading extension, it is called by the word Virgo; and then, because it stands in perfect balance (_samatva_) in mid-palate, it takes the form of Libra — and just by that balance it merits [the name] _viṣuvat_ (equinox), 'that which deserves pervasion.'"

sections.title: 11. The "Archer" Haṃsa returning to the heart-lotus (7.117–119)

lines: ṣaḍaṅgulād adhastāt tu dhanvisthaś carate hṛdi |
hṛtpadmāntaṃ tu vai haṃsaś caritvā ūrdhvagodayaḥ || 7-118 ||

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Leaving Scorpio behind, the crossing into Sagittarius is declared; below the six finger-breadths, standing in Sagittarius, it moves in the heart. Having coursed as far as the end of the **heart-lotus**, the **Haṃsa** [again] rises upward. Thus, at the twelve crossings beginning with Capricorn, it moves forever; and by just this sequence [is measured] the **life-span of all embodied beings**."

**Commentary.** "**'Below'** — resorting to the lower six finger-breadths, it 'moves in the heart,' i.e., comes to rest (_viśrāmyati_). And there this **Haṃsa**, because its target is now fixed (_baddha-lakṣya_), is called 'the Archer' (_dhanvin_ = Sagittarius). … Having coursed to the end of the heart-lotus, the Haṃsa **again takes up the [ascending] activity of prāṇa**." — On 7.119: "At the crossings that fall in Capricorn and the rest, the **Haṃsa** courses through the twelve — that is, the months beginning with Māgha — always, at every breath-movement; and this lasts _'the life-span of all embodied beings,'_ i.e., as long as one lives."

lines: prāṇahaṃsagatiṃ cāre jñātvaikasmiṃs tu tad bhajet || 7-142 ||

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Having **known the course of the Prāṇa-Haṃsa** in [each single] breath-movement, one should then undertake that [rite — an eclipse-practice, etc.] within a single [breath]."

**Commentary.** "The Haṃsa-hood of the breath is **as before** (i.e., per 7.29). _'In the course'_ — in the flow of _prāṇa_ and _apāna_, which encompasses the pervasion up to the sixty-year cycle. _'That'_ means the lunar eclipse and the like." _(Because the entire macrocosm of Time is folded into one breath, the adept who reads the Prāṇa-Haṃsa's motion can perform in one breath what outwardly awaits an eclipse.)_

sections.title: 13. As the Haṃsa courses, so it reckons the world as Time (7.144–146)

lines: yathā caraty asau haṃso jagaty asmiṃś carācare || 7-145 ||

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Again I shall declare, by the division of the three channels — in the southern, northern, and equinoctial course — **how this Haṃsa courses** through this world of moving and unmoving things, dwelling within as **Time itself** (_kāla-rūpeṇa_), **reckoning the world by its measures** (_kalābhiḥ kalayan jagat_), taking the three channels as its support, established on the three pathways."

**Commentary.** "…Now [I shall tell] how the **Haṃsa** courses in the equinox that is the right, the left, and both together — in the world made of the moving and the unmoving: moving among moving beings, and, by the mode of the outgoing of the senses, **touching even unmoving things**; and therefore _'dwelling within'_ the [various] subjects, **fixing its foot as Time** — past, present and future — **reckoning the whole world** by its measures (_kalā_: instants, _tuṭis_, _lavas_, etc.), emitting and withdrawing it by way of the sixfold transformation beginning with birth. Even in an unmoving thing, this indwelling Haṃsa, by joining the sap in the right, left, and central channels, effects the nourishment of flower and fruit — so say the knowers of the science of plant-life (_vṛkṣāyurveda_)."

Verses 7.147ff. then unfold this Haṃsa as "supported on the three channels, established on the three paths, invaded by the three guṇas, set in the three states [waking/dream/deep sleep], overrun by the six causal-lords, joined with the three powers [icchā-jñāna-kriyā], lying between moon, sun and fire" — i.e. the single Haṃsa differentiated through the whole yogic physiology.

sections.title: 14. The Prāṇa-Haṃsa crossing the twenty-four saṃkrāntis (7.167, 7.170)

lines: bāhye caiva tv ahorātre adhyātmaṃ tu varānane |

blocks.s: **Translation.** "In one outer day-and-night — that is, in the inner [breath-day] — the **Prāṇa-Haṃsa** crosses **twenty-four transitions** (_saṃkrānti_)."

**Commentary.** "By the mere contact with the three principal channels of the eight-petalled heart-lotus, it is thus [twenty-four] — so say the knowers of pervasion. _'Prāṇa-Haṃsa' as before._" _(Twelve by day, twelve by night.)_

lines: śatāni nava vai haṃsa ekām ekāṃ vahet sadā || 7-170 ||

blocks.s: **Translation.** "The twenty-four transitions, [in one] of balanced humours, by [the breath's] own nature: the **Haṃsa** carries each single [transition] as **nine hundred** [breaths], always." _(Kṣemarāja's gloss: in a healthy body the Haṃsa moves each saṃkrānti at a steady 900 breath-counts; deviation from this signals what is desired or undesired, and — developed in the death-omen sections — impending death.)_

sections.title: 15. The Kāla-Haṃsa and the conquest of death (7.206–211)

blocks.s: The chapter's climactic Haṃsa teaching: meditation on the Haṃsa as Lord of Time (Kāla-haṃsa / Svacchanda) conquers death and confers omniscience.

lines: evaṃ śarīraje kāle mṛtyuṃ cāśubham eva ca |
jñātvā yogī jayen mṛtyum aśubhāny apy aśeṣataḥ || 7-206 ||

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Thus, having **known** death and misfortune in the body-born [reckoning of] Time, the yogin conquers death, and misfortunes too, entirely — having **meditated on Svacchanda, the Lord of Time, or on the Haṃsa, the Lord of the manifest** (_sakaleśvara_). Abiding on the pathway of the nostril-aperture, he **emits and withdraws the world**; abiding therein he **reckons** (_kalayet_) all, established in all beings."

**Commentary.** "Having meditated on — that is, made vivid by the technique of entering-into — **Svacchanda, the Lord of Time**, who at will illumines all of Time in its divisions (gross, subtle, and so on) and in its outer and inner forms; the **Haṃsa** whose nature is the supreme partless [Lord] as already explained, the Lord of the whole manifest world — the yogin conquers death: this is the link with what precedes.

"…**'Nose'** (_nāsikā_) is the central Power, [derived] from _nasate_, 'moves crookedly'; on the pathway of its aperture, in the _suṣumnā_ abode, [the Lord] — having by the descending sequence assumed the form of breath — stands in the nose and in the apertures (the hollow zones of the eyes and the other senses); and by the mode of opening and closing (_unmeṣa-nimeṣa_) he emits and withdraws the world, outer and inner. Abiding there, he **reckons all**: he casts the inwardly-fixed outward, and the outwardly-manifest inward; and he 'reckons' — that is, arranges variously, knows, and reflectively apprehends — since the root _kal_ means to cast, to count, to go, and to know."

lines: kālahaṃsaṃ sa tu japan dhyāyan vāpi maheśvari |
sa bhavet kālarūpī vai svacchandaḥ kālavac caret || 7-210 ||

blocks.s: **Translation.** "**Reciting** the **Kāla-Haṃsa** (_kāla-haṃsa_), or even **meditating** on it, O Great Goddess, he becomes one who has **the very form of Time** — [he becomes] **Svacchanda** — and he moves about **like Time** [freely]: his death slain, having cast off old age, freed of all fear [that comes] from diseases."

**Commentary.** "The **Haṃsa** whose self is the supreme partless Lord, determined before — that very one, **reckoning the universe by way of the nature of abandoning-and-taking-in** (_hāna-samādāna_) already settled, is here called the **Kāla-Haṃsa**, the Time-Haṃsa.

"**'Reciting or meditating on it'** — reciting by repeating the utterance of the mantra of the Four-_Kalā_ Lord (_catuṣkala-bhaṭṭāraka_), being intent again and again on repose in it, through contemplation of the pervasion taught in the connecting-passage of the section on the Five Praṇavas. **'Having the form of Time'** — he for whom there arises this eminent form of Time, whose essence is the reckoning of the entire universe, becomes verily the Lord **Svacchandabhairava**. And he wanders about just like [Time], ever proceeding through the **performance of the fivefold act** (_pañcavidha-kṛtya_). By the fear caused by diseases — of that he is freed."

Verse 7.211 then lists the fruits: "hearing from afar, thinking, seeing [at a distance], and the attainment of all the qualities of sovereignty (aiśvarya) — these arise ever from the conquest of Time (kāla-jaya)." Kṣemarāja: through absorption into the nature of the Haṃsa — Svacchandabhairava beyond all space-and-time, pervading every aperture — the yogin transcends body and senses, and, re-flooded by the savour of the Supreme Reality, is as-if-automatically free of aging, death, disease, and the limits of finite knowledge.

sections.title: 16. The Haṃsa meditated in the three channels as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra (commentary on 7.212–216)

blocks.s: The verses (7.212–216) assign the fruits of right-, left-, and central-channel meditation. The Uddyota makes the Haṃsa explicit.

lines: … bhaviṣyajjño bhaved vāme viṣṇutulyabalaś ca saḥ || 7-213 ||
… bhūtaṃ bhavyaṃ bhaviṣyac ca sarvaṃ jānāti madhyataḥ || 7-214 ||

blocks.s: **Translation (gist).** "Meditating in the **right** nostril he gains Brahmā's sovereignty [and knowledge of the past]; in the **left**, he knows the future and is equal in strength to Viṣṇu; from the **middle**, he knows all — past, present, and future — and by constant meditative practice attains equality with Rudra… By the supreme mode he gains the station of Īśvara, of Sadāśiva, and [meditating on] the supreme being of Rudra, one becomes **Śiva**."

**Commentary.** "As was said before [7.151], _'Brahmā and Īśvara stand on the right, Viṣṇu and Sadāśiva on the left, Rudra and Śiva are declared in the middle'_ — the abiding of the six causal-lords in the three channels alone, by the higher and lower pervasion. Therefore, if in the right and left channels one **meditates on and reflectively realizes the Haṃsa in the form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra** by the lower pervasion, then one becomes possessed of their strength, virility, and sovereignty, and knows the threefold-time universe; and by meditating on Brahmā and the rest, through the higher pervasion, as Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva, one attains their very nature."

sections.title: 17. The Haṃsa raining nectar — the amṛta-meditation (7.217–226)

blocks.s: A distinct death-conquering practice: visualizing a Haṃsa in an inverted lotus at the palate, raining immortal nectar down through the channels.

**Translation.** "…For one who meditates on the **nectar**, [there is] victory [over death]. Having meditated on the **heart-lotus** of sixteen petals — set at the aperture of the channel-stalk, white, in full bloom, endowed with the sixteen _kalās_, a **full moon** with all its digits complete, its form the pericarp — one should contemplate in its midst the **Self**, pure and stainless as crystal… Above [is] a second lotus in a great ocean of _śākta_ nectar; and that lotus **faces downward**, its pericarp a full moon. **In its midst one should contemplate the Haṃsa**, downward, tipped with the _bindu_-flame, **raining down divine nectar** (_varṣantam amṛtaṃ divyam_) — one should visualize it [flooding] on every side."

The visualization continues (7.222–225): the nectar, entering by the upward channel-aperture of the Self, floods and fills the whole body through the mouths of all the channels bound to the lotus-stalk, so that "the whole body is filled with nectar." "Thus the one ever yoked becomes equal to the Lord of Nectar (Amṛteśa), and — casting off diseases, death and old age — sports with the powers beginning with aṇimā." (7.225)
**Translation.** "Thus, from this **meditation on the nectar**, victory over Time-and-Death is his."

**Commentary (summary).** Kṣemarāja glosses the whole as a single image: an adept who for six months continuously contemplates the crystal-bright **Self** within the moon-filled heart-lotus, and above it the downward-facing **Haṃsa** in the inverted palatal lotus — from whose four-_kalā bindu_-radiance the stream of nectar pours through the _brahmarandhra_ and floods every channel-mouth of the body — "becomes free of disease, un-aging and undying, endowed with the _siddhis_ beginning with aṇimā, and equal to **Amṛteśa-Bhairava**." He adds that the nectar here (_amṛta_) is "the essence of the bliss of the Supreme Power" (_paraśakti-ānanda-sāra_). He then frames the sequel: "Having thus taught the conquest of death both by the **Haṃsa-meditation** resting on all three channel-paths and by the **nectar-meditation**, [the text] now begins to teach the truly ultimate essence" — namely the _athavā_ option (7.226): "**Or else, one established in the Supreme Reality is not afflicted by any of the Times.**"

In the closing yoga-teaching, Bhairava names the supreme secret and prescribes seated practice of the Haṃsa-Svacchanda by way of the tenfold yoga (the six purifications, retention, withdrawal, fixation, meditation).

lines: saṅkalpya kalpanālakṣyaṃ dhyāyed vai tena sarvagam |

blocks.s: **Translation.** "By the tenfold path of yoga one should practise the **Haṃsa-Svacchanda**. Having conceived the **mantra** as that which has passed beyond the _bindu_, its form the radiance at the end of _nāda_ — [an object] beyond [ordinary] conceiving (_kalpanā-alakṣya_) — one should meditate through it upon the **all-pervading** [Haṃsa-Svacchanda]."

**Commentary.** "**'By the tenfold path of yoga'** means: by the six practices — outer and inner exhalation and the rest — [culminating in] the quiescent retention (_praśānta-kumbhaka_), withdrawal (_pratyāhāra_), fixation (_dhāraṇā_), and meditation (_dhyāna_) that are to come; and, having first conquered the tenfold vital airs (_prāṇa_ and the rest), one should practise — that is, **enter into** — the aforesaid **Haṃsa-Svacchanda, the partless Lord** (_niṣkala-bhaṭṭāraka_).

"He clarifies that entering: uttering the mantra of the Four-_Kalā_ Lord beginning with the _a_-_kalā_, then transcending the _bindu_ — thereby unsealing the station of the checking-power (_nirodhikā_) that is the half-moon — and by the sequence of _nāda_ and _nāda-anta_ reaching the form of radiance that is the light of the Power and beyond; having, after [initial] conceptualization, reached it **non-conceptually**; the all-pervading **Haṃsa-Svacchanda**, unmarked by [any] mental construction, self-luminous dense mass of consciousness-and-bliss — this one should meditate on, **dissolving it up to the** **_samanā_** **level**, and enter it by the dawning of an **uncreated reflective awareness** (_akṛtaka-vimarśa_)."

The chapter then turns to nāḍī-purification and prāṇāyāma as the supports of this practice, closing (7.315): "One should first conquer the breath; when the breath is conquered, the mind is conquered; and when the mind is conquered, for the tranquil one the Supreme Reality shines forth."

The chapter closes: _"iti śrīsvacchandatantre … śrīkṣemarājaviracitoddyotākhyavyākhyopete kālādhikāraḥ nāma saptamaḥ paṭalaḥ"_ — "the seventh chapter, named the Section on Time, in the _Svacchandatantra_, together with the commentary called _Uddyota_ composed by the venerable Kṣemarāja." Kṣemarāja's own summary verse restates the whole: _"Having rightly known the universe as resting within the breath, through the pervasion that is the outspreading of consciousness, one should — by the knowledge of the portions [of Time] — attain the full, [ever-]abiding [state], [together with] the several siddhis."_

The verse text follows the _Uddyota_ edition as transmitted in the source; a few readings there are visibly corrupt (e.g. _mirayeta_ for _mriyeta_, _nirṇeṣyamāṇan_ etc.), and where a form was plainly a scribal slip I have silently read the standard form in the translation while leaving the transliteration close to the copy. Passages purely concerned with breath-arithmetic that surround a Haṃsa line have been summarized in italics rather than translated in full, to keep the Haṃsa thread continuous.

This is a short Kaula revelation-text in the standard dialogue frame: the Goddess asks, Bhairava answers. Its subject is the _haṃsa_ — the Self as the spontaneous, unrecited breath-mantra _haṃsa/so'ham_ moving in the three channels — treated first as an object of visionary sight (verses 4–20), then as the ground of _kālajñāna_, the reading of mortality in signs (21–29), and finally as the secret technique for cheating Time altogether (30–40). The remainder is the _samaya_ frame: who may receive this and who may not.

The manuscript is in poor condition. The verse numbering collapses after v. 40 and restarts at 32; I have renumbered continuously in square brackets and given the manuscript number where it differs. Asterisks and question marks in the source mark illegible _akṣaras_. Where the reading is genuinely uncertain I have translated conservatively and flagged it in the notes rather than emending silently.

Oṃ, homage to Śiva — to him who is Śiva, the giver of what is auspicious, homage and homage again. Oṃ, homage to the Supreme Self. Oṃ, homage to the Remover of Obstacles. Here the _Haṃsasāra_ is set down.

lines: śrutaṃ deva mayā pūrvam amalaṃ haṃsayāmalam |
punar hi śrotum icchāmi sārāt sārataraṃ param ||

blocks.s: O God, I have heard before the immaculate _Haṃsayāmala_. Now I wish to hear again what is beyond it — more essential than the essence.

lines: yat purā kathitaṃ deva sūcitaṃ na prakāśitam |
vada me vastu sadbhāvaṃ prasādaṃ kuru śūlabhṛt ||

blocks.s: What was told before, O God, was only hinted at, never disclosed. Speak to me the true being of the Real. Grant your favour, Bearer of the Trident.
Well asked, well asked, O greatly wise one, awakener of all beings to their purpose. For that very purpose I shall declare it fully, out of love for you, Maheśvarī.

lines: yo 'sau śānto hy ajo devaḥ śaktyādhāro hy avigrahaḥ ||

blocks.s: It is hard to come by, even for all the gods, and for the yoginīs likewise. That God who is at peace, unborn, the support of Śakti, having no body —

lines: ca caiṣa paramo haṃsaḥ sa vai devaḥ sanātanaḥ ||

blocks.s: — he abides always as the living being itself, travelling in the left, the right, and the middle. This is the supreme Haṃsa; he alone is the everlasting God.

lines: sa brahmā sa ca vai rudra īśvaro viṣṇur eva ca |
sadāśivaḥ paraṃdhāma tārakaṃ brahma eva ca ||

blocks.s: He is Brahmā, he is Rudra, Īśvara and Viṣṇu as well; he is Sadāśiva, the highest abode, and the Brahman that carries one across.

lines: vārāṇasyāṃ tu deveśi svakaṃ mārgaṃ prakāśitam |

blocks.s: But in Vārāṇasī, Mistress of the gods, my own path has been made manifest. That field is [the undoing of] ignorance; for those who know, it stands without need of vows.

lines: lakṣaṇaṃ tasya vakṣyāmi yena jñāsyanti sādhakāḥ |
gurvavasthā gamaḥ so hi dṛśyate na tu lakṣyate ||

blocks.s: I shall state the mark of it, by which sādhakas will recognise it. Its coming is the guru's own condition: it is seen, and yet cannot be marked out.

sections.title: III. The Nature of the Haṃsa (9–20)

lines: sa paraḥ sarvato hy ātmā cañcalatve vyavasthitaḥ |

blocks.s: He is the supreme Self on every side, established in the very condition of tremor. Standing without and within, he vibrates in all embodied beings.
Perpetually risen and perpetually settled, without beginning, lord of the end; unmanifest and yet possessed of manifest form; ungraspable; moving and unmoving at once.
He is grasped through contemplative feeling; he is consciousness alone, and stands firm by the power of consciousness. The Lord, whose form is radiance, the Supreme, abides in the sky of the heart.

lines: śuddha sphaṭikasaṅkāśaṃ bhinnaṃ vyomni tu vyomavat ||

blocks.s: Standing in the outer sky he is smoke-coloured; at the smoke's edge his body is Nature herself. Then he appears like clear crystal — distinct within the void, and yet like the void.
The vine of liberation takes that shape, resembling a shimmering, variegated coil. It has the look of a bee — the syllable HA, headless, unstruck.

lines: siddhoti nūnaṃ tat tasmiñciva puṣpāṇi paśyati ||

blocks.s: The Lord of the Kula, supreme and at peace, is seen as the unbroken succession of the Kula. Then surely he is accomplished — for therein he sees the flowers of Śiva.
He is seen through the division of the one into many, through ten million divisions. The Supreme Lord is seen through the partitioning into manifold forms.

lines: havito piṅgalo dīpto niśi veśmani dṛśyate |

blocks.s: Tawny, blazing, he is seen in the house at night. Having the form of the light of the real void, he sounds forth again and again.

lines: sa bāhyābhyantaraṃ lakṣyaṃ yo dadāti dine dine |
aghaṃśamaya te devi na kvacidyoni sambhavaḥ ||

blocks.s: He who day after day yields this sign, outer and inner alike, quenches sin, O Goddess: there is for him no birth from any womb.

lines: tasya cāpaścimaṃ janma haṃso dṛśyo varānane ||

blocks.s: For one intent upon devotion to Śiva through thousands of successive births — for him this birth is the last, and the Haṃsa becomes visible, O lovely-faced one.

lines: kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin dṛṣṭe parāpare ||

blocks.s: The knot of the heart is split, all doubts are severed, and his actions are worn away — when that supreme-and-not-supreme is seen.

lines: pṛthivyāṃ nāsti tad dravyaṃ yad datvā cāriṇī *? vet ||

blocks.s: The teacher who bestows knowledge of the Haṃsa is truly hard to find. There is no substance on earth which, by giving it, one could [repay him].
Now I shall declare the knowledge of Time, O Mother — the full understanding of Time's signs, so that yogins do not fall into the lower courses.

lines: taṃ dṛṣṭvāpi ciraṃ devi punarjanma na vidyate ||

blocks.s: Coiled in the shape of a serpent, in front, throughout all the filaments: having beheld that even briefly, O Goddess, no further birth is found.
If it takes the form of a liṅga, one attains release; if it is dense, there will be bondage. When it is red one should know the body is frail; when yellow, wealth is coming.

lines: subhikṣaṃ ca pracāre ca durbhikṣaṃ cañcu bandhane ||

blocks.s: With serpent-forms, an extraordinary journey — the grace of _bindu_ and _nāda_. Plenty when it moves freely; famine when the beak is bound.

lines: tridivairdivase yukte mriyate ca tato dhruvam ||

blocks.s: If it is severed in the middle, he dies within three months — no doubt of it. If three days are joined to the day, he dies thereafter for certain.

lines: pūrvāhṇe pūrvasaṃsthaṃ tu yathā dṛṣṭvā varānane |

blocks.s: Having seen it in the forenoon, stationed to the east, O lovely-faced one, the discerning practitioner should contemplate it in a cupped handful brimming with water.
Established [in the moon-channel], if it passes to the right, one should predict death within six months. By the division of moon and sun one should observe day and night.

lines: dvau māsau somasūryābhyāṃ māsaṃ somasya dakṣiṇe |

blocks.s: Two months by moon and sun together; one month when the moon is in the right. Eastward and rightward, on the new moon, it enters the solar orb.
**29.** _somāvasyāṃ daśāhetu pañcāhaṃ sūryagottare | ekaḥ kālasya paryāyaṃ kathitaṃ tava sundari ||_
Ten days at the lunar new moon; five days when the sun goes northward. One full cycle of Time has now been told to you, O beautiful one.

lines: kālasya vañcanaṃ deva kathaṃ jānāti tattvataḥ |

blocks.s: **[The Goddess:]** But how, O God, does one truly know the outwitting of Time? Speak to this doubt — my eagerness rests here.

lines: śṛṇu devi paraṃ guhyaṃ rahasyaṃ bhuvi durlabham |
yanna kasya cidākhyātaṃ tat te vakṣyāmi suvrate ||

blocks.s: **[Bhairava:]** Listen, Goddess, to the highest secret, the mystery hard to find on earth, which has been told to no one. That I shall tell you, O you of good observance.
In the centre of the lunar orb one should contemplate the syllable ṬHA, beloved. The Haṃsa, gone into the middle of ṬHA, is to be contemplated with full effort.
**33.** _brahmarandhrātsravantī ca paramāmṛtarūpiṇī | avyayā sarvagā sūkṣmā parā cāsya parākalā ||_
And flowing down from the brahmarandhra, having the form of the supreme nectar — imperishable, all-pervading, subtle, transcendent — is his highest _kalā_.
**34.** _haṃsodara gatā sā tu sravantī cintayet priye | kālo na kalayeccātra na jarāvyādhireva ca ||_
One should contemplate her streaming, gone into the belly of the Haṃsa, beloved. Here Time does not count him out, nor does old age, nor disease.
This outwitting of Time, O Goddess honoured by the heroes, must be kept hidden. The Mothers desire the nearness of one who guards it, O mistress of sādhakas.
