blocks.s: Therefore, with every care, it is not to be given to just anyone. It is to be given to those joined with devotion, whose very selves delight in devotion to the guru.

lines: yo guruḥ sa śivaḥ sākṣāt pūjanīyaḥ prayatnataḥ ||

blocks.s: The guru is to be known as one who has gone into Śiva; and Śiva is what issues from the guru's mouth. Whoever is the guru, he is Śiva in person, to be worshipped with diligence.

lines: tasya jñānaṃ ca mokṣaṃ ca siddhyate paramārthataḥ ||

blocks.s: Pure, capable, disciplined — and his śakti flooded through with That: for such a one, knowledge and liberation are accomplished in the ultimate sense.

lines: tasmin sthāne yadā līnaṃ cittaṃ vigatavṛttikam |

blocks.s: When the mind, its fluctuations gone, dissolves into that place, within six months he will be freed of wrinkles and grey hair.

lines: na kālaṃ kalayeccātra na ca sāvyādhireva ca |
haṃsasāraṃ paraṃ brahma paraṃ vyoma paraḥ śivaḥ ||

blocks.s: Here Time does not count him out, nor disease either. The essence of the Haṃsa is the supreme Brahman, the supreme Void, the supreme Śiva.
The manuscript's numbering restarts here; MS numbers given in parentheses.
For your welfare this compendium, the _Haṃsasāra_, has been proclaimed. It is not to be given to the faithless, the treacherous, the cruel of mind —
— to hypocrites, to the undevoted, to those whose hearts delight in mere Tantric observance. For they are bound beasts, vermin, cast out from the Great Path.
Burnt up by hesitation and discursive thought, tormented by the blindness of great delusion, unassured, unsatisfied, formed by the scriptures of the bound.
They do not attain the Supreme — that turbulence teeming with masses of great waves, the incomparable all-in-all of the Stream, come to rest in the guru's mouth.
Therefore, O you honoured by the heroes, with every care it is to be given to one devoted to the guru, at peace, delighting in unceasing practice —
**[46]** (MS 36) _vīrācāraniṣaṇṇāya dravyādvaitaparāya ca | samayā sevine nityaṃ kulakālodite śive ||_
— to one seated firmly in the observance of the heroes, given over to the non-duality of substances, ever serving the _samaya_, in the Śiva who rises at the Kula hour;
— to one without pretence, discreet, delighting in concealed observance. For [the Mothers] abide in the form of their own rays, coming from the seats, embodied as the seats themselves.
For those forever free of error, they take on the manner of acting unseen; possessed by compassion, they protect the keepers of _samaya_ observance.
With their whole being and with effort, the Mothers cause to unfold, in the midst of the breath, that supreme radiance which is gathered within.
Themselves unimpelled, they impel the attainments beginning with _melāpa_. For the heroes he stands in perceptible form, both without and within.
By the awareness of the yogins whose hearts [are opened], within the Kaula teaching: the secret, the going-forth to what is to be known — here the ground is one that reaches the unfathomable.
And the secret of liberation-while-living, easily come by for the lords of heroes, has been declared — the entire essence, supreme, [spoken by Hara] together with Umā.

lines: tasmāt sarvaprayatnena na deyaṃ yasya kasyacit ||

blocks.s: The goal is a hidden cavern, sought for the most part by hundreds and by thousands [in vain]. Therefore with every care it is not to be given to just anyone.
This knowledge is for a single disciple, not to be divulged by the great-souled. It lies outside all scripture — the Heart within the Kula of the Yoginīs.

**v. 5** — _vāmadakṣiṇamadhyagaḥ_: the standard triad of _iḍā_, _piṅgalā_, _suṣumnā_. The _jīvabhūtaḥ_ construction is doctrinally pointed: the bodiless (_avigraha_) Śiva of v. 4 _is_ the living being, not merely its cause. The stray _ca ca_ at the start of pāda c is metrically defective; likely a scribal doubling.

**v. 7** — _jñānināmavrataḥ sthitam_ is unmetrical and probably corrupt. I read _avrataḥ_ as "without [obligatory] vows," i.e. Kāśī grants what elsewhere requires observance. An alternative is _a-vrataiḥ_, "even by those without vows."

**v. 8** — _gurvavasthāgamaḥ_ is ambiguous between "its coming is the guru's condition" and "the transmission (_āgama_) of the guru's state." The second half is the clearer claim, and a familiar one: the Haṃsa is available to sight (_dṛśyate_) but resists definitional marking (_na lakṣyate_) — perception without _savikalpa_ determination.
**v. 10** — _nityodita_ is the Kashmirian technical term par excellence; _niṣṭa_ is presumably for _niṣṭha_ / _niṣṭhita_, giving the standard pairing of perpetual arising with perpetual repose.

**v. 11** — _caitanyāsusthitaḥ_ is the crux. I have taken it as _caitanyāt su-sthitaḥ_. Reading _asu-sthitaḥ_ ("established in the vital breath") is also possible and fits the breath-context of the whole text rather well; I flag it because it would materially change the verse.

**v. 13** — _aśirāhatam_ resists confident construal. _A-śiras_ would describe the _ha_-glyph deprived of its headstroke; _anāhata_ would give the familiar "unstruck sound." The bee-simile (_bhramareṇa pratīkāśam_) supports the acoustic reading — the humming _ha_ — so I have kept both senses in the translation rather than choosing.

**v. 16** — _havito_ is unconstruable as it stands. Something like _kapilaḥ_ or a form of _huta-_ would fit the colour-sequence (tawny/blazing). The nocturnal indoor vision here belongs to the same visionary-diagnostic register as the _kālajñāna_ section that follows.

**v. 19** — A near-verbatim echo of _Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad_ 2.2.8, with _parāvare_ replaced by _parāpare_ — the substitution is doctrinally deliberate, importing the Śaiva _para/parāpara/apara_ triad into the Upaniṣadic formula.

**v. 20** — Both damaged points are recoverable in sense if not in letter: _\*vidaiśikaḥ_ is almost certainly _deśikaḥ_ with a preceding syllable lost, and the second half is a topos (nothing on earth suffices to repay such a teacher), so the missing verb is likely a form meaning "could requite."

**vv. 23–29** — This is a compressed _chāyā_-divination and breath-divination manual and the most damaged stretch of the text. The signs are read from a visionary form (shape: serpentine, liṅga-like, dense; colour: red, yellow) and from which nostril-channel the breath runs relative to the solar and lunar orbs. My renderings of 27–29 give the sense of the numerical scheme but the correspondences do not fully cohere as transmitted; _somasūya_ in 27 is for _soma-sūrya_, and _sūryagottare_ in 29 is probably _sūryago 'ttare_.

**v. 32** — ṬHA is the conventional tantric cipher for the lunar disc, so the instruction is self-referential: visualise the moon within the moon, and the Haṃsa at its centre. This verse plus 33–34 is the whole technique for "cheating Time" — the nectar streaming from the _brahmarandhra_ is caught in the belly of the Haṃsa rather than falling into the solar fire.

**v. 42** — _tantrācāraratātmanām_ listed among the disqualified is not a scribal slip. It reflects the standard Kaula hierarchy in which the _tantra-prakriyā_ is a lower dispensation than the _kula-prakriyā_; devotion to ritual observance alone marks one as still a _paśu_.

**v. 44** — _ogha_ here is the Kaula "stream" or current of transmission (as in _divyaugha_, _siddhaugha_, _mānavaugha_), not simply "flood," though the wave-imagery of the preceding pāda plays on both.

**v. 49** — _yadvāntasambhṛtam_ admits two readings: _yad vānta-sambhṛtam_, "nourished by what has been emitted," which would carry the Kaula sacramental sense; or _yad vā antaḥ-sambhṛtam_, "or rather, gathered within." I have taken the second as the more likely, given that the radiance is being unfolded _prāṇa-madhye_, but the first cannot be excluded in a text of this affiliation.

**v. 50** — Badly corrupt. _te nodito nodayanti_ is unconstruable; my rendering assumes a play on _na-udita / unnodayanti_ ("themselves unimpelled, they impel"), which suits the surrounding sense but is a guess. Note the number-disagreement in pāda c–d (_pratyakṣarūpo_ singular against _sthitāḥ_ plural), which I have not smoothed over.

**v. 52** — _umayāsaharaṃ param_ is metrically and grammatically broken. The most economical restoration is _umayā saha haraṃ param_, "supreme Hara together with Umā," which would make this a standard colophon-style attribution of the dialogue.

The passages Parts III and IV lean on beyond ST 7 and the _Haṃsasāra_, quoted as given in unpublished working translations. Each is cited by text, verse and the file it comes from. Bracketed notes are the manual's, not the translator's.
**Sūtra.** _madhya-vikāsāc cid-ānanda-lābhaḥ ||_
"The attainment of the bliss of consciousness (cid-ānanda-lābha) arises from the expansion of the center (madhya-vikāsa)."

**From the commentary.** _sā tu māyā-daśāyām tathābhūtāpi svarūpaṃ gūhayitvā prāk saṃvit-prāṇe pariṇatā iti nītyā prāṇa-śakti-bhūmiṃ svīkṛtya avarohakrameṇa buddhi-dehādi-bhuvam adhiśayānā nāḍī-sahasra-saraṇim anusṛtā …_

"In the stage of māyā, that same consciousness hides her true form and becomes the vital force (prāṇa-śakti). Descending (avarohakrama), she pervades intellect, body, and the network of subtle channels (nāḍī-sahasra-saraṇi)."
_evaṃbhūtāpi eṣā paśūnāṃ nimīlita-svarūpa eva sthitā_ — "In bound beings, this central consciousness remains dormant, with its true nature closed off."

"When, by the means already described, the Goddess Consciousness (saṃvid-bhagavatī), existing as the innermost center (madhya-bhūtā), unfolds, or when the madhya itself — the central brahma-nāḍī — expands, then from that expansion arises the attainment of the aforesaid cidānanda (bliss of consciousness). Thence follows the jīvanmukti already explained."
[_prāk saṃvit prāṇe pariṇatā_, "consciousness first becomes breath," is a citation inside the commentary on sūtra 17; the mentor guide's "PH 17" refers to this line.]
**Sūtra.** _vikalpa-kṣaya-śakti-saṃkoca-vikāsa-vāha-ccheda-ādi-anta-koṭi-nibhāla-nādaya iha upāyāḥ ||_

"Here the means [to the unfolding of the centre] are: the dissolution of thought-constructs (_vikalpa-kṣaya_), the contraction and expansion of power (_śakti-saṃkoca-vikāsa_), the cutting of the currents [of breath] (_vāha-ccheda_), attentive contemplation of the first and last points [of the breath] (_ādi-anta-koṭi-nibhālana_), and so on."
**On setting aside mechanical methods.** _prāṇāyāma-mudrā-bandhādi-samasta-yantra-troṭanena sukhopāyameva hṛdaye nihita-cittaḥ…_
"By transcending all mechanical methods such as prāṇāyāma, mudrā, and bandha, one should place awareness at ease within the heart (hṛdaye nihita-cittaḥ)."
**On the breath's start and end points.** _ādikoṭiḥ hṛdayam antakoṭiḥ dvādaśāntaḥ tayoḥ prāṇollāsa-viśrānti-avasare nibhālanaṃ citta-niveśanena pariśīlanam |_

"The initial limit (ādi-koṭi) is the heart (hṛdaya); the final limit (anta-koṭi) is the dvādaśānta (a point roughly twelve finger-breadths above the crown). One should contemplate at the moment between the rising and resting of the breath, fixing awareness (citta-niveśa) alternately upon these two points."

[Corrected 1 November 2026. The folder's rendering of the sūtra read _ādi-anta-koṭi-nibhālana_ as "methods reaching up to the supreme limit"; it is rendered here to match Kṣemārāja's own gloss below, attention to the heart and the _dvādaśānta_. The folder's note credits this line to Abhinavagupta; the _Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya_ and its commentary are by Kṣemārāja.]

**Translation of the verse and the opening of the** **_Parimala_** (new working translation from the Sanskrit e-text, Muktabodha M00035, Trivandrum Sanskrit Series 66; to be checked before handouts). This fills the gap in the folder's translation, which began partway through the commentary.
"If you wish to ascertain the welling-up of your own heart, eternal and partless, then the middle tuṭi of moon and sun, as they reach their release (_astra_), must be snapped." (56)

"Now, about to teach the very clear means, beginning with the āṇava, to the reflective awareness of the vibrancy of the Self's nature established above, he first discloses all three in a single verse.

"'Your own heart' is the heart fit to be directly realized, whose nature has already been explained. Its 'welling-up' is its flashing forth in the variety of object and subject and the rest. By nature that is 'partless', because it excludes the division of time, and free of the stain of every construct, such as what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted. If you who have approached [as disciples] feel some wish to make it, so described, the ground of a certainty that has the wonder of direct perception, with utter clarity (for, as the _Bhagavad Gītā_ says, 'a person is made of faith; as one's faith is, so is one'), then here is the means. This construal holds for all the meanings to be given.

"Moon and sun are the phonemes _sa_ and _ha_: the moon because it animates all that is known, the sun because it is the knower, undivided from the Akula sun. Their _astra_ is the visarga, and their _āsthā_ is the anusvāra, which marks enclosing [them] in one's heart. As the two reach these, the tuṭi in the middle (the instant in which they stand apart, a fragment of time) must be snapped out, extracted as [a letter is extracted] in the _Mālinī_ and the like. Then the awareness '_haṃsa_' arises. The idea is this: although in reciting the alphabet _ha_ and _sa_ are taken like any other letters, that pair, inseparable from the Anuttara in one's heart, should be contemplated, by fusing them, as the great mantra _haṃsa_: a means to recognize one's own Self as _ahaṃ saḥ_, 'I am He'. The mantra is extracted in reverse order, [as _so'ham_]:
"'Dealing outwardly with worldly people, concealing what lies within reach of reasoning, moving by the path of disguise, one should lead [the disciple] up, as on the left-hand way.'"
The folder's translation picks up from here.
**From the commentary, as translated.**

"Thus, in keeping with the disciplinary line of the Śrī Laghu-bṛṃhaṇī, he brings in 'so'ham' both to signal the requirement of secrecy and to point the reader toward another mantra. And because this practice takes the form of reflexive awareness focused on particular mantra-phonemes, it is a certain āṇava means. As the Mālinīvijaya says: the samāveśa that arises through arranging utterance, bodily placement, visualization, phoneme, and locus is called the properly āṇava (mode of entry). The same should be understood with respect to 'uccāra' and the rest.

"Here 'uccāra' is the activity of prāṇa—whether breath is retained, exhaled, or filled; at the end of it, that state called 'śānta' shines as stilled through stillness. 'Karaṇa' is a bodily settling (postural/physiological placement); 'dhyāna' is an inner sketching of awareness; and 'sthāna-kalpana' is configuring loci such as the mūlādhāra—at the root a golden heap, in the heart a lightning-flash, at the ājñā a moonlike radiance. Even if these sometimes blend, one should note which factor predominates.

"Moreover, 'soma' is the object-side surge, thick with the character of seeking, knowing, and doing; 'sūrya' is the flashing of the means of knowledge, consisting of will, knowledge, and action. While these two are reaching their respective efficacies, the 'truṭi' belonging to me—the Self as knower—appears as a fault in the form of doubt; it must be snapped, i.e., the doubt that rises in relation to the Self must be cut through. For this coarse blossoming of the world—animated by seeking and so forth—never occurs without the activity of the triad of powers (will/knowledge/action). Therefore one drives away the panic of doubt, which is precisely the inversion of clear, immediate realization; and thereby one gains the heart-centered reflexive awareness described above. Insofar as it can be effected without utterance and the rest—simply as subtle configurations within awareness itself—this is a Śākta means, as that very text says: the samāveśa attained by contemplating the reality by mind alone, without uccāra, is called Śākta.

"Again, it is also taught that soma is apāna and sūrya is prāṇa, moving from dvādaśānta to the heart and from the heart to dvādaśānta. In the middle 'tuṭi'—marked as both outer and inner—where the two naturally arrive at a flashing characterized as a 'throw' (kṣepa), one should rupture into that act of reflexive awareness, whose mark is camatkāra (astonished savor), until it becomes fully heart-penetrating and decisively known. Though the recognition of prāṇa and apāna as ever-arisen, common to the whole body, and as a simultaneous double-release like the fire-drill sticks is already established, it should be deliberately linked for the sake of stabilizing heart-joy and camatkāra; yet even if one doesn't link it, its reality is not harmed.

"This means, however, is to be understood as Śāmbhava, since it operates by eliminating all turbulence of conceptualization and by establishing only one's own nature; hence: 'The āveśa that arises in one who thinks of nothing at all, when awakened by the guru, is called Śāmbhava.' Some also explain it, following Vijñānabhairava-style reasoning, as extracting by intelligence the tiniest sliver of time that lies between the moon and the sun. But the author doesn't press that here. Because of the force of vernacular usage the tantra speaks in shorthand: 'astram—let it go,' 'astam—the middle,' 'mama—tuṭi,' 'struṭi—snap.'

"Finally, these three means inevitably intermix when examined closely; they are distinguished only by which is predominant. And one should not imagine any difference in the fruit of awareness: all upāyas culminate in the same result; distinctions are pedagogical, made for the sake of gathering and guiding students. Hence the standard map: Śāmbhava and Śākta are the nondual means; Āṇava is the dual or mixed means. The more 'prāṇa-grounded' ones are accomplished through uccāra and related techniques; the intermediate ones through purified conceptual formations; the subtlest through those same formations once pacified."

**1.23.** _yām avasthāṃ samālambya yad ayaṃ mama vakṣyati | tad avaśyaṃ kariṣye 'ham iti saṃkalpya tiṣṭhati ||_ "Seizing that state of poised receptivity and resolving, 'Whatever he (the guru, or inner Self) instructs, that I shall surely do,' the aspirant stands firmly established."

**1.24.** _tām āśritya ūrdhva-mārgeṇa soma-sūryāv ubhāv api | sauṣumṇe 'dhvany astamito hitvā brahmāṇḍa-gocaram ||_ "Relying on that state and turning upward along the central path, the two luminaries — sun and moon — sink within the suṣumṇā, as the yogin leaves behind the sphere of the cosmos (the bodily universe)."

**1.25.** _tadā tasmin mahā-vyomni pralīna-śaśi-bhāskare | sauṣupta-padavan mūḍhaḥ prabuddhaḥ syād anāvṛtaḥ ||_ "Then, in that vast expanse where the sun and moon are set, he appears outwardly inert like one in deep sleep, yet inwardly he is awakened and unobscured."

**Transition to 1.26.** _evaṃ spanda-tattvasya udayaḥ proktaḥ | tadā asmād eva ca sahajaḥ mantra-udayaḥ |_ "Thus the arising (udaya) of the spanda-tattva has been explained. From that very realization there then arises the innate manifestation of mantra (sahaja-mantrōdaya)."

**1.26.** _tad ākramya balaṃ mantrāḥ sarva-jña-bala-śālinaḥ | pravartante 'dhikārāya karaṇānīva dehinām ||_ "Having entered into that supreme power—the radiance of pure, unobstructed consciousness—the mantras, filled with omniscient potency, function for their appointed purposes, just as the organs of action operate for embodied beings."
**Scriptures cited in the commentary on 1.26.**

_Haṃsa-Pārameśvara: paśu-bhāve sthitā mantrāḥ kevalā varṇa-rūpiṇaḥ | sauṣumṇe 'dhvany uccaritāḥ patitvaṃ prāpnuvanti te ||_ "Mantras that remain in the bound state (_paśu-bhāva_) are mere letters; uttered on the path of the suṣumṇā, they attain lordship." [Corrected 1 November 2026: the folder renders _patitvaṃ_ as "flightlessness (fall)"; it is _pati-tva_, "lordship", which is what the argument requires.]

Śrī Vaihāyasya-Saṃhitā: viṣuvat-sthaṃ japaṃ kuryād nāda-ūrdhva-dhvani-bodhitam | mantrākṣarāṇi maṇivat śaktau protāni bhāvayet || tāmeva ca pare vyomni paramāmṛta-bṛṃhitām | darśayaty ātma-sad-bhāvam evaṃ mantro huti-vinā ||

"He should perform japa at the equinoctial (balanced) point, aware of the upward resonance of nāda; he should contemplate the mantra-syllables as jewels strung on śakti, and see that śakti, expanded with the supreme nectar in the higher sky, revealing the very being of the Self—thus the mantra yields realization without any outer offering."

sections.title: C6. Kṣemarāja, Spanda Sandoha on Spandakārikā 1.1

blocks.s: **From the commentary.** "Here, in the case of the Supreme Lord — whose nature is pure and constituted of the Great Light (mahā-prakāśa-ātman) — there exists but one single power of reflexive awareness (parāmarśa-śakti). When appearing as a faint movement (kiṃcid-calattā-ābhāsa-rūpa), it is called by many names in the Āgamas: spanda (vibration), sphurattā (radiance), ūrmi (wave), bala (power), udyoga (effort), hṛdaya (heart), sāra (essence), mālinī, parā, and countless others. Though single, this one power is simultaneously unmeṣa-nimeṣa-mayī — made up of both the opening and closing movements."

sections.title: C7. Tantrāloka 6 with Jayaratha's Viveka: the haṃsa passages

blocks.s: **Source.** _Tantrāloka_ of Abhinavagupta with the _Viveka_ of Jayaratha, KSTS edition, chapter 6 (_kālatattvaprakāśana_, "illuminating the principle of time"), from the Google Doc "Tantraloka 6" in the Tantrik Translations folder. The file's opening line reads "aṣṭhamāhnikam", a slip for _ṣaṣṭham āhnikam_.

**How to read this section.** The Sanskrit is quoted as it stands in the file. The English is a new working translation made for this manual (1 November 2026), as literal as readability allows; square brackets mark words supplied for sense. It has not yet been checked by Jacob or Nataraj Chaitanya, so mark it "draft" on any handout until it has. Abhinavagupta's root verses seldom name the haṃsa; almost every use of the word comes in verses of _Svacchandatantra_ 7 that Jayaratha quotes, so the chapter mainly shows how the Trika read ST 7 (Appendix A).

sections.title: C7.1 THE TOPKNOT AS ATTENTION TO EVERY BREATH (TA 6.22–23)

blocks.s: From the _Viveka_:

lines: ayameva hi śikhābandho yatprāṇaśakteḥ praticāramādimadhyānteṣvavadhānena punaḥ punaḥ parāmarśanaṃ nāma | yadabhiprāyeṇaiva -- "ṣaṭ śātāni divā rātrau sahasrāṇyekaviṃśatiḥ | japo devyāḥ samuddiṣṭaḥ sulabho durlabho jaḍaiḥ ||" (vi. bhai. 156) ityādyanyatroktaṃ

blocks.s: **Translation (6.22cd–23).** "But when it is bound at the time of worship and the like, it is of the nature of Śiva, because it is partless. For within a day and night its course is twenty-fourfold, bringing manifold fruits through [units of] hundreds of breath-movements counted as 'openings' [i.e. nine hundred]."

**Translation (****_Viveka_****).** "This alone is the binding of the topknot: reflecting again and again on the power of breath, with attention at the beginning, middle and end of every single breath. It is with this very intention that it is said elsewhere: 'Six hundred and twenty-one thousand, by day and by night: this is declared the japa of the Goddess, easy, yet hard for the dull' (VBh 156)."

**Note.** The topknot (_śikhā_) is the power of action; "tying" it before worship is reread as attention to the breath. Jayaratha also quotes ST 7.57 here: "Even when the mind is placed elsewhere and the eye is cast elsewhere, the breath goes on of itself, without effort, always." This is the closest TA 6 comes to a statement of ajapā practice.

sections.title: C7.2 THE THREE JUNCTURES INSIDE ONE BREATH (TA 6.24–27)

lines: kṣapā śaśī tathāpāno nāda ekatra tiṣṭhati || 6-24 ||

blocks.s: **Translation (6.24–27).** "Where night, the moon, the apāna and nāda stand together in one place, and the sun of the life-breath does not rise: such a half-tuṭi is the twilight. (24–25ab) When the sun faces upward, the moon faces downward and fire is in between, the midday [twilight] grants liberation, with the sun standing in the middle of the sky; for its essence is boundless and it awakens the whole circle of beings. (25cd–26) Where bindu, the breath, the day and the sun stand together in one place, the third, the great twilight, abides, utterly at peace. (27)"

**Note.** Each breath has its own dawn, noon and dusk. The first twilight is the pause after the in-breath has come to rest in the heart; the third is the pause after the out-breath has come to rest outside. "Its essence is boundless" renders _anantamitasāraḥ_, whose sense is uncertain. This is a usable image for Part III: the pause at each turn of the breath is a twilight.

sections.title: C7.3 PRACTICE AT THE MOMENT OF ECLIPSE (TA 6.107–108)

blocks.s: **Translation (6.107–108).** "Bathing, meditation, oblation, japa and the like, [done] in the interval between the seizing and the release, bear great fruit, worldly and beyond the world, [and] in the world to come. (107) Entering for an instant into the dissolution of the agitation of devourer and devoured, one who performs meditation, worship and the like at an eclipse of the moon or sun shares in liberation. (108)"
**Note.** The eclipse is internal: the moment where the moon-breath and the sun-breath swallow one another. Jayaratha glosses "devourer and devoured" as knower and known, and cites ST 7.74.

sections.title: C7.4 THE HAṂSA'S COURSE MAKES THE CALENDAR (TA 6.110–116, VIVEKA)

lines: "prāṇahaṃso yadā prāptastvadhastātprathamāṃ tuṭim | pūrvamardhaṃ tvahaḥ proktaṃ tuṭyardhamaparaṃ niśā ||" (7|77)

"śaktyadho hṛdaye haṃsaḥ saṃkrāmetkarkaṭe priye | ṣaḍaṅgulāni saṃtyajya siṃhe vai saṃkrametpunaḥ || ṣaḍaṅgulaiḥ punastyaktaiḥ kanyāṃ saṃkramate punaḥ | nāsikāgrāttu tālvantaṃ tyakte vai viṣuvadbhavet || tulāsaṃkrāntireṣoktā dakṣiṇaṃ viṣuvadbhavet ||" (svaṭaṃ. 7|113)

blocks.s: **Translation (ST 7.77, quoted on 6.111).** "When the breath-haṃsa has reached the first tuṭi below, the first half is called day, the [other] half of the tuṭi night."

**Translation (ST 7.113, quoted on 6.116).** "Below Śakti, in the heart, the haṃsa enters Cancer, dear one; leaving six finger-breadths, it enters Leo; when six more finger-breadths are left, it enters Virgo; when [the stretch] from the tip of the nose to the end of the palate is left, the equinox occurs. This is called the passage into Libra; it is the southern equinox."
**Note.** Every outer calendar point has an inner counterpart within one breath. For the manual this is background; Part IV already tells mentees not to teach the breath arithmetic to newcomers.

sections.title: C7.5 ONE BREATH IS ENOUGH (TA 6.128, VIVEKA)

lines: yaśchedastatra yaḥ sandhiḥ sa puṇyo dhyānapūjane || 6-128 ||

blocks.s: From the _Viveka_, quoting ST 7.140:

lines: "... dhyānayogatapobhiśca bāhye kāle'tha yatkṛtam | amunokte varārohe tatphalaṃ labhate mahat || prāṇahaṃsagatiṃ cāre jñātvaikasmiṃstu tadbhajet |" (svaṭaṃ. 7|140)

blocks.s: **Translation (6.128).** "The juncture where a watch, day, night, month, season, year, twelve-year cycle or sixty-year cycle ends: that juncture is holy for meditation and worship."

**Translation (ST 7.140, quoted in the** **_Viveka_****).** "…whatever is done with meditation, yoga and austerities at an outer time, O lovely one, [the yogin] described here obtains that great fruit. Knowing the course of the breath-haṃsa within its movement, let him practise it in a single [breath]."

**Note.** Jayaratha's point is that what outer ritual might not finish in a lifetime, the yogin reaches by a moment's attention within one breath. This is the strongest support in TA 6 for the claim in Part III that the practice goes with you in every breath.

sections.title: C7.6 NINE HUNDRED BREATHS PER TRANSIT (TA 6.199–200)

blocks.s: **Translation (6.199cd–200ab).** "Carrying the nine hundred breaths contained in two and a half _nāḍikās_, it moves twenty-fourfold through the day and night."
**Translation (ST 7.168, quoted).** "In one of even constitution there are by nature twenty-four transits; the haṃsa always carries nine hundred [breaths] in each one."
**Note.** 900 × 24 = 21,600. These are the same ST 7 verses as in Appendix A.

sections.title: C8. Vijñānabhairava with Ānandabhaṭṭa's Vijñānakaumudī: the breath and haṃsa verses

blocks.s: Note that verse numbers differ between editions. The file numbers the haṃsa-mantra verse "54" where the run of verses calls for 154, and numbers the next half-verse 155. Other editions, and the mentor guide, count these as 155–156.
These are the first four of the 112 _dhāraṇās_. They all turn on the two points where the breath turns: the heart, and the _dvādaśānta_, twelve finger-breadths beyond the body.

lines: ūrdhve prāṇo hyadho jīvo visargātmā paroccaret |

blocks.s: **Gist.** The out-breath (_prāṇa_) goes up and out, the in-breath (_jīva_) comes down and in, and the supreme, whose nature is emission, utters itself as both. By holding attention at the two places where each breath arises, one comes to rest in fullness. The _Kaumudī_ places the two points at the _dvādaśānta_ and the heart, and says this attention leads to the self-awareness "I" (_aham_) once every adjunct is forgotten. This is the verse closest to ajapā-haṃsa and the best one to set beside ST 7.59 (Appendix A §5).
**Gist.** By following the breath, inward or outward, to the two "spaces" where it turns, the body of Bhairava is revealed. The _Kaumudī_: the two spaces are the _dvādaśānta_ and the heart.

**Gist.** When the breath-power neither goes out nor comes in, it opens up; in that middle, free of thought, one takes on Bhairava's form. This is the pause itself. It matches the "twilights" of TA 6.24–27 (C7.2).

lines: kumbhitā recitā vāpi pūritā vā yadā bhavet |

blocks.s: **Gist.** Whether the breath is held, emptied or filled, at its end the power called "Peace" shines, and through it the Peaceful One. The _Kaumudī_ compares the settling to a potter's wheel slowing after the push. It also quotes the _Pratyabhijñā_: resting in one's own nature is the awareness "I am he" (_so'ham_).

sections.title: C8.2 THE MEETING OF THE TWO BREATHS (VBH 64)

blocks.s: **Gist.** Where the two breaths meet, inside or outside, the yogin becomes the vessel in which the knowledge of sameness (_samatva_) dawns. The _Kaumudī_ places the meeting at the heart and the _dvādaśānta_.

sections.title: C8.3 "I AM THE SUPREME HAṂSA" (KAUMUDĪ ON VBH 65 AND 91)

blocks.s: On verse 91, which is about meditating on oneself as boundless space, Ānandabhaṭṭa quotes:

**Gist.** "I alone am the supreme haṃsa, the supreme Self, beyond the beyond." He also uses the line in his comment on verse 65. This is not a breath practice, but it shows the haṃsa as a name for the Self, as in ST 7.29–30 (Appendix A §2).

sections.title: C8.4 THE HAṂSA MANTRA THAT EVERY BEING REPEATS (VBH 152–156 IN THE FILE'S NUMBERING)

lines: dīrghātmā sā mahādevī paraṃ kṣetraṃ parātparā || 152 ||

blocks.s: **Gist.** The out-breath goes and the in-breath enters by will (_icchā_), as the curved, long-drawn Great Goddess, the supreme field. Whoever moves and rests in her, on that path made of great bliss, is filled by the goddess and reaches the supreme Bhairava. Day and night the living being repeats the mantra "haṃsa, haṃsa" 21,600 times; this is called the goddess's japa, very hard to grasp at the end of the breath. On 152 the _Kaumudī_ declines to explain, saying the secret meaning is set out in the _Tantrāloka_ and must be learned from a teacher. It glosses "the end of the breath" as the state of coming to rest (_paryavasāna_).

**A difference between the readings.** This edition's second line, "_prāṇasyānte sudurlabhaḥ_" ("very hard to grasp, at the end of the breath"), agrees with the line as Kṣemarāja quotes it in the _Uddyota_ on ST 7.56 (Appendix A §3). Jayaratha on TA 6.23 (C7.1) quotes it differently, as "_sulabho durlabho jaḍaiḥ_" ("easy, yet hard for the dull"). This edition also lacks the half-verse that other editions give here, "_sakāreṇa bahir yāti hakāreṇa viśet punaḥ_" (with _sa_ it goes out, with _ha_ it comes back in), which the mentor guide cites as VBh 155. If you quote that half-verse to students, say that it is missing from the KSTS text.

sections.title: C9. More from the Mahārthamañjarī and the two Mahānayaprakāśas

blocks.s: These are Krama texts. The Krama reads the breath as the place where time is devoured: the out-breath and in-breath are sun and moon, and practice is their dissolution into the ground "beyond breath" (_aprāṇabhūmi_). That is the same move as ST 7's conquest of time (Appendix A §15), described from the side of the goddess Kālī.

sections.title: C9.1 THE RARE TEACHER (HAṂSABHEDA, QUOTED IN THE PARIMALA'S INTRODUCTION)

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Many teachers are served, shining with knowledge and understanding; but rare, O Goddess, is the teacher who brings about the destruction of the ego. He has studied, he has listened, he has done everything, who, freed from ego, has known the Alone by himself."

**Note.** The text quoted is called the _Haṃsabheda_. It echoes _Haṃsasāra_ 20 (Appendix B), on the rarity of the teacher who gives knowledge of the haṃsa. It is useful for Part V on what a teacher is for.

sections.title: C9.2 THE ROYAL SWAN OF THE MIND (MANONUŚĀSANASTOTRA, QUOTED IN THE PARIMALA ON MM 2)

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Swans, when they fly, always spread their two wings. But your flight, O royal swan of the mind, in the supreme sky is a great wonder, for you have left behind the pair of wings made of distraction and blankness."

**Note.** _Mānasa-rājahaṃsa_ is a pun: the royal swan of Lake Mānasa, and the royal swan of the mind (_mānasa_). Ordinary attention flies on two wings, being scattered and going blank; the mind's swan flies without either. Maheśvarānanda says the verse is by his own teacher. It is a ready image for the articulation exercises (Part III).

lines: akālakalite vyomni spandamānā tu yā citi |
kālaṃ grasati dehāntaḥ śmaśānaṃ sa tathā smṛtaḥ || 2/16 ||
kālagrasanaśīlatvāt tvak śmaśānaṃ tu sā bahiḥ || 2/17 ||

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Consciousness, pulsing in the space that time does not measure, is the one ground where time is burned: she is held to be the cremation ground, Khecarī. (15) In the state where nothing is known, in those who sleep, the breath, endowed with the power of pulsation, devours time within the body; so it too is called the cremation ground. (16) Time, which is the reckoning of what is known, also comes to an end [there]. Because it habitually devours time, the skin is the outer cremation ground. (17)"
**Note.** Even in deep sleep the breath keeps "eating" time. This is the Krama form of ST 7.59, the haṃsa that utters itself with no one uttering it.

sections.title: C9.4 COUNTING IS NOT KNOWING (ANONYMOUS MAHĀNAYAPRAKĀŚA 7.184–187)

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Through the sequence of the breath, made of the division of word and meaning, the light of consciousness shines as unsequenced utterance. (184) This sequenced [breath] stands near the unsequenced utterance, not far from it, as its general form. (185) Those who leave aside their own experience in this way and, just to fill out the numbers, loudly expound [the Self's] nature in a haphazard way through the knots, supports and kalās of the cakras, the order of the letters and other incoherent methods: they too are not possessed of knowledge. (186–187)"

**Note.** This is a classical warning against teaching the breath as arithmetic or as a map of centres at the expense of experience. It supports the guardrail in Part IV and the use/avoid table in Part III.

sections.title: C9.5 THE BREATH DISSOLVES INTO THE GROUND BEYOND BREATH (ŚITIKAṆṬHA, MAHĀNAYAPRAKĀŚA)

blocks.s: On verse 3 of the opening (p. 7 of the KSTS text):

lines: kālo bhairavaḥ, sa ca nādasvabhāvaḥ prāṇarūpaḥ, yaduktam — sthāvaraṃ jaṅgamaṃ caiva sarvaṃ prāṇasya bhojanam || iti, bhairavāyamāṇaṃ taṃ prāṇaṃ bhakṣayitvā vilāpya aprāṇabhūmiṃ nādanidhanamāsādya

blocks.s: **Translation.** "Time is Bhairava, and its nature is sound (_nāda_) and its form is breath. As it is said: 'Everything, moving and unmoving, is food for the breath.' [The goddess] devours that breath which is acting as Bhairava, dissolves it, and reaches the ground beyond breath, where sound comes to its end."
From the section on the three cremation grounds (p. 52):

lines: grāsakāḥ prāṇāśca kāliśarīraṃ spṛśanti tatra viśrāmyanti iti kālagrāso dvitīyaṃ śmaśānam … prāṇasya kulābhyantara evāprāṇabhūmau upaśamo dvitīyam

blocks.s: **Translation.** "The devourers, the breaths, touch the body of Kālī and come to rest there: this devouring of time is the second cremation ground … The second is the stilling of the breath within the Kula itself, in the ground beyond breath."
From the section on the order of awareness (p. 102):
**Translation.** "…because prāṇa and apāna, which are Śiva and Śakti, and the self, all of them constructing and constructed, set in the ground beyond breath when one stops constructing them."
And, on sun and moon (p. 83):

lines: prāṇo hi sūryaḥ, apānaścandramāḥ, dinaṃ sūryo, rātriścenduḥ, piṅgalā sūryaḥ, iḍā candramāḥ

blocks.s: **Translation.** "For prāṇa is the sun and apāna the moon; the day is the sun and the night the moon; piṅgalā is the sun and iḍā the moon."

**Note.** This is the same pairing of sun with prāṇa and moon with apāna as MM 56 (C3) and ST 7. Śitikaṇṭha adds the goal: the pair dissolves into the stillness "beyond breath". Use it for mentors' study, not for beginners; the Kālī imagery needs context.
